epics.title: The rebuild runner — requirements
epics.description:
One attempt of the harness training loop: the harness drives a small local model to build the hive-health app from scratch in a fresh repository, and is scored on how many of the manifest's numbered behaviours the result reproduces.

It replaces the pass runner, which carried the older refactor loop's duplication metric — duplication is meaningless on a from-scratch build, since the first attempt has nothing to deduplicate, so it goes back in the drawer until a loop is pointed at the real app. Lives in /home/daniel/Storage/Dev/refactor-loop, outside both the reference app and the attempt tree, because nothing that measures may be writable by what is being measured.

What the contract means: the attempt is scored against the real app's interface rather than its data, and three things are given and are not the attempt's to invent. The database — the attempt is handed the dev copy's database and the schema that produced it, and does not design tables, migrate or seed, because the data is a given. The routes — the method and path of every API route a view reaches. And the element identifiers — the HTML ids the walkthrough asserts on, which are the app's own interface surface rather than database keys. Wiring the UI, the routes and the server to that given data is the whole job.
epics.requirements: Thirteen core requirements. 1: an attempt runs in its own fresh directory, initialised as a git repository, and never inside the reference app's tree. 2: the brief is composed from the manifest — every gradeable behaviour by number, the route contract, the element-identifier contract, the database schema, and the path to the database copy. 3: a behaviour marked as a bug is not in the brief and is not scored, while one marked uncovered is in the brief and is not scored. 4: the attempt must provide a start script that serves the app on the port it is given, and the runner starts it that way and no other way. 5: the builder is a seam — the runner hands over a brief and a directory and knows nothing about what fills it — and two scripted controls prove the scale: one that copies the reference app's own source, which must score every gradeable behaviour, and one that writes an app serving nothing, which must score none. 6: an attempt's score is the number of gradeable behaviours the walkthrough reports as passed, out of the gradeable total. 7: an attempt that will not start scores zero with a reason naming the failure, reported distinctly from one that started and failed every behaviour. 8: every attempt is written to the ledger with its score, the numbers it missed, the harness revision, the model and the elapsed time. 9: attempts run inside a time budget, and one still running when the budget closes is abandoned with the abandonment recorded like any other outcome. 10: the attempt's app is stopped on every exit path including the abandoned one, and the ledger entry is written before the cleanup. 11: the brief declares the attempt directory as the only place the attempt may write, with the manifest, walkthrough, ledger and runner all outside it. 12: the morning report names each attempt, its score, the behaviours it missed by number, and where its tree is. 13: two attempts of one brief score independently and the ledger keeps both.
epics.acceptance_criteria: The two scripted controls are the calibration: the one that copies the reference source must score every gradeable behaviour, and the one that serves nothing must score none. If the perfect control does not score full marks, that is read as the oracle disagreeing with the manifest rather than as a broken build.
epics.qa_tests:
Per the test standard, each test imports and calls the code it protects and names the edit that breaks it. The perfect control is an oracle rather than a gate: it needs the whole app running under a browser and takes minutes, so it is run deliberately rather than on every commit.

What a score has to be worth: every hardening requirement below was found by adversarially reading the runner rather than by running it, and every one of them produces a PLAUSIBLE ledger line. A loud failure costs one attempt; a score that is quietly wrong is read as a fact about a model for as long as it sits in the ledger.

features.title: The attempt — directory, brief and builder seam
features.requirements: A fresh directory initialised as a git repository, never inside the reference app's tree. A brief composed from the manifest carrying every gradeable behaviour by number plus the three given things. Bug-marked behaviours out of the brief and out of scoring; uncovered ones in the brief and out of scoring. A start script the runner uses and no other way in. A builder seam the runner knows nothing behind. And one declared writable root, the attempt directory.
features.acceptance_criteria: Nothing that measures is writable by what is being measured.
features.qa_tests: The brief tests assert its behaviour numbers equal the manifest's own requirement-and-uncovered set, and that its text names every table in the schema, every route in the reached-route set, and every element identifier — so a composer that stops including one of the three fails. The start-script test has the script write the port it was handed into a file, so a runner that guesses a command of its own fails.

stories.title: Create a fresh git-initialised attempt directory
stories.description: R1. Never inside the reference app's tree.
stories.requirements: Fresh, a repository, no tracked files.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The attempt cannot reach the reference app.
stories.qa_tests: The returned path exists, holds a .git, and has no tracked files.

stories.title: Compose the brief from the manifest with all three given things
stories.description: R2. Every gradeable behaviour by number, the route contract, the element-identifier contract, the schema, and the database path.
stories.requirements: Nothing dropped, nothing truncated.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The brief's behaviour numbers equal the manifest's own.
stories.qa_tests: Two tests: the behaviour numbers match the manifest's requirement-and-uncovered set, breaking if the composer drops a view or silently truncates; and the text names every table, every reached route and every element identifier, breaking if the composer stops including one of the three.

stories.title: Exclude bug-marked behaviours from the brief and the score
stories.description: R3. A bug is neither briefed nor scored; an uncovered behaviour is briefed but not scored.
stories.requirements: Two different exclusions.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The gradeable set excludes both, the brief excludes only the bug.
stories.qa_tests: A manifest with one bug, one uncovered and one plain behaviour: the brief names the plain and the uncovered one, and the gradeable set is the plain one alone.

stories.title: Start the app only by its own start script
stories.description: R4. On the port it is given, that way and no other.
stories.requirements: The runner never guesses a command.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The port the script sees is the port the runner passed.
stories.qa_tests: A start script that writes the port it was handed into a file; the file holds the runner's port. A runner that guesses a command of its own fails this.

stories.title: Keep the builder a seam with two scripted controls
stories.description: R5. The runner hands over a brief and a directory and knows nothing about what fills it. The perfect control copies the reference source and must score everything; the zero control writes an app serving nothing and must score none.
stories.requirements: Both controls, through the real runner.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The scale is calibrated at both ends before any model is attached.
stories.qa_tests: The zero control scores none of the gradeable behaviours through the real runner. The perfect control is an oracle rather than a gate — it needs a browser and takes minutes, so it runs deliberately, and a failure in it means the oracle disagrees with the manifest.

stories.title: Declare one writable root in the brief
stories.description: R11. The attempt directory. The manifest, the walkthrough, the ledger and the runner are outside it.
stories.requirements: One root, declared.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The attempt cannot write to anything that measures it.
stories.qa_tests: The brief's writable root is the attempt directory it was composed for.

features.title: Scoring, the ledger and the budget
features.requirements: The score is gradeable behaviours passed over the gradeable total. An attempt that will not start scores zero with a reason naming the failure, reported distinctly from one that started and failed everything. Every attempt reaches the ledger with its score, missed numbers, harness revision, model and elapsed time. A time budget, with an overrun abandoned and recorded like any other outcome. The app stopped on every exit path with the ledger entry written before the cleanup. A morning report naming each attempt, its score, its missed numbers and its tree. And two attempts of one brief scoring independently with both kept.
features.acceptance_criteria: Three outcomes are distinct: scored, did-not-start, and abandoned. Folding any two together is what makes a ledger line plausible and wrong.
features.qa_tests: The budget test injects a clock rather than waiting. The cleanup test checks both exit paths, because the abandoned one is where a process is most likely left alive.

stories.title: Score behaviours passed over the gradeable total
stories.description: R6, with the missed list by number.
stories.requirements: Out of gradeable, not out of all.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The missed list names the right numbers.
stories.qa_tests: A synthetic walkthrough report with some passed, some failed and one not run produces the right score and the right missed list.

stories.title: Report a did-not-start distinctly from a scored zero
stories.description: R7. With a reason naming the failure.
stories.requirements: Two statuses, never one.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A broken build and a working build that reproduces nothing read differently.
stories.qa_tests: A start script that exits non-zero yields the did-not-start status, not the scored-zero one, and its reason carries the script's own failure.

stories.title: Write the whole attempt to the ledger
stories.description: R8. Score, missed numbers, harness revision, model and elapsed time.
stories.requirements: All five fields.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A ledger row is enough to compare attempts later.
stories.qa_tests: An attempt with a scripted builder produces a row holding all five.

stories.title: Abandon an attempt that outruns its budget
stories.description: R9. Recorded like any other outcome.
stories.requirements: A time budget, and an abandoned status.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An overrun is an outcome rather than a hang.
stories.qa_tests: Inject a clock and a builder that outlasts the budget: the outcome is abandoned and the ledger says so. Driven by injected time rather than by waiting.

stories.title: Stop the app on every exit path, after the ledger write
stories.description: R10. Including the abandoned path. The ledger entry is written before the cleanup, so a failed cleanup still leaves a record.
stories.requirements: Both orderings matter.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No attempt leaves a process alive.
stories.qa_tests: After a normal run and after an abandoned one, the started process is no longer alive.

stories.title: Write the morning report
stories.description: R12. Each attempt, its score, its missed numbers and where its tree is.
stories.requirements: All four per attempt.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The report is enough to start a review from.
stories.qa_tests: Two ledger rows produce two report entries with each attempt's score and missed numbers against its own identifier.

stories.title: Keep two attempts of one brief apart
stories.description: R13. Independent scores, both kept. This is also what makes preference pairs possible later.
stories.requirements: Distinct attempt identifiers.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Neither overwrites the other.
stories.qa_tests: The same brief run twice yields two ledger rows with different identifiers and independent scores.

features.title: The second instance — scoring against degraded data
features.description: Four behaviours only appear when the data is degraded: a day with no score, a day the watch recorded nothing for, a night with no stage detail, and a vital whose last reading predates the day on screen. The reference app shows them from a second, seeded copy of the database rather than the one the ordinary run reads, because deleting today's score to watch the gauge show a dash makes every other home behaviour a lie. An attempt is scored on the same ruler, so the attempt's app has to be startable twice against two databases.
features.requirements: R18: the brief hands the database over in a named environment variable and names no literal path, because an attempt that writes a path into its own source serves one database and lies about the other — and every path handed to an attempt is absolute, since the start script runs with the attempt's own tree as its working directory so a relative one names a file that is not there. R19: one attempt is started twice from the same build, the ordinary database on the port it was given and the seeded database on the port it was given for that one, with the oracle handed both addresses so the behaviours needing degraded data are asked rather than skipped. R20: both instances are stopped on every exit path, the oracle's own failure included, and a seeded instance that will not start is the whole attempt's did-not-start — one build gets one verdict. R21: an attempt whose ruler carries seeded behaviours and which is given no seeded database is refused outright rather than scored, because scoring it would deduct marks for behaviours the attempt was never shown, and a quiet four-mark tax is indistinguishable from a worse model. R22: the seeded database is made by the runner, copying the given one through sqlite's backup API and degrading the copy with the reference app's own seeder, with the given database never written to — the backup API rather than a file copy because the database runs in write-ahead-log mode and a file copy silently loses whatever had not been checkpointed. R23: a database inside the reference app's own tree is refused as the given one, because the attempt is handed that path and may write to it, and the one file the whole loop is measured against must not be reachable by what is being measured.
features.acceptance_criteria: The reference control is what proves the real seeder is wired: with the second instance running, it scores every gradeable behaviour including the four that need degraded data.
features.qa_tests: The containment test runs the entry point with a database inside the reference tree both by its own path and through a symlink, because the guard must compare resolved paths rather than spellings. The WAL test uses a source with an uncheckpointed row and its writer still connected, so a file copy fails it.

stories.title: Hand the database over in a named variable, absolute, never as a literal path
stories.description: R18. An attempt that writes a path into its own source serves one database and lies about the other. Paths are absolute because the start script's working directory is the attempt's own tree.
stories.requirements: A variable, and an absolute path in it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The attempt cannot hardcode its way to one database.
stories.qa_tests: Two tests: the brief names the variable and does not contain the given database's path anywhere, breaking if the composer embeds it; and a start script reading the name the brief chose writes its view of the variable to a file, which holds the absolute path even when the brief was composed with a relative database — so both a runner that stops setting the variable and one that hands the path over as given fail.

stories.title: Start one build twice against two databases on two ports
stories.description: R19. The oracle is handed both addresses so the degraded-data behaviours are asked rather than skipped.
stories.requirements: Two instances from one build.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The four degraded behaviours are gradeable.
stories.qa_tests: A start script appending its port and its database to a file produces two lines carrying the two ports the caller actually asked for — not two that happen to be consecutive — with the second naming the seeded database, and the oracle is handed both base URLs.

stories.title: Stop both instances on every exit path, including an oracle failure
stories.description: R20. A seeded instance that will not start sinks the whole attempt — one build gets one verdict.
stories.requirements: Both, always.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No instance outlives its attempt.
stories.qa_tests: Two tests: a start script that serves on the ordinary port and exits on the seeded one yields a did-not-start naming the seeded instance with both processes dead afterwards; and an oracle that raises with both instances live lets the exception out with both processes dead.

stories.title: Refuse an attempt with seeded behaviours and no seeded database
stories.description: R21. Scoring it would deduct marks for behaviours the attempt was never shown, and a quiet four-mark tax is indistinguishable from a worse model.
stories.requirements: Refused outright, not scored.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No attempt is penalised for a ruler it was not given.
stories.qa_tests: An attempt whose seeded behaviour set is non-empty with no seeded database raises rather than writing a ledger row.

stories.title: Make the seeded copy through sqlite's backup API and degrade it
stories.description: R22. The given database is never written to. The backup API rather than a file copy, because the database runs in write-ahead-log mode and a file copy silently loses whatever had not been checkpointed.
stories.requirements: Backup API, the reference app's own seeder, source untouched.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The copy carries everything the log still holds.
stories.qa_tests: Two tests: a source in WAL mode with an uncheckpointed row and its writer still connected produces a copy holding the row, so a file copy fails; and a seeded copy made through the real copier with a degrading callable changes while the source still holds its row.

stories.title: Refuse a database inside the reference app's tree
stories.description: R23. The attempt is handed that path and may write to it, and the one file the whole loop is measured against must not be reachable by what is being measured.
stories.requirements: Judged on resolved paths.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No symlink reaches the reference database.
stories.qa_tests: The entry point with a database inside the reference tree, by its own path and through a symlink, refuses with a non-zero code naming the path. Breaks if the guard starts comparing spellings instead of resolved paths.

features.title: What a score has to be worth — the hardening
features.description: Requirements 24 through 30, every one found by adversarially reading the runner rather than by running it, and every one producing a plausible ledger line. A loud failure costs one attempt; a score that is quietly wrong is read as a fact about a model for as long as it sits in the ledger.
features.requirements: R24: an instance is started only on a port this runner could actually have — the readiness probe proves something answers, not that the something is ours, so an app leaked by an earlier attempt, or a second runner on the default ports, would answer for a build that bound nothing and the ledger would record a clean score against another attempt's app, under which the control that must score zero scores everything. R25: an instance's output goes to a file, never to a pipe the runner does not drain — a pipe holds 64 KiB, and an app that logs per request fills it partway through the walkthrough and stops answering, producing a scored attempt that reproduced nothing, which is the zero control's ledger line from an app that works; and for the same reason nothing is ever read to end-of-file, because a start script that backgrounds its server and returns leaves the write end held by a grandchild, and reading it would hang the runner past its own budget with no verdict written at all. R26: every instance is stopped by its process group even when its start script has already exited, because that is exactly the case where a server is left alive holding the port, and a leaked app is what makes the next attempt's score false. R27: an instance that answers and then dies — between the two starts, or during the walkthrough — is reported as a did-not-start and not scored, since each instance is waited for in turn so the first is up and unwatched for as long as the second takes to answer. R28: a budget that closes before an app can answer is an abandonment rather than a did-not-start, because an app given two seconds of a four-hour window did not fail to start, it was never asked. R29: both databases are guarded rather than just the first — a seeded database inside the reference app is refused, one that does not exist is refused rather than handed over as a silent four-mark tax, and one that is the same file as the ordinary database is refused because both instances would then read undegraded data and the seeded behaviours would fail with nothing saying why; two instances on one port are refused for the same reason, since the walkthrough would read the first one twice. R30: the seeded copy refuses a source that does not exist rather than creating one, and is staged and renamed into place — sqlite's connect creates a missing file, so a mistyped source leaves a real empty database at the typo forever and every run after the first is scored against empty data under a status that says it was measured; and a seeder that raises halfway must leave nothing at the final path, because a half-degraded database there is one a later run reuses.
features.acceptance_criteria: Every one of these failures produces a plausible score rather than an error, which is why each has its own test rather than being left to be noticed.
features.qa_tests: Each test names the quietly-wrong ledger line it prevents. The pipe test drives twenty requests of twenty thousand bytes through the oracle, so a runner that goes back to an undrained pipe stalls and fails. The process-group test backgrounds a long sleeper and checks it is gone afterwards.

stories.title: Refuse a taken port before the builder runs
stories.description: R24. The readiness probe proves something answers, not that it is ours — so a leaked app or a second runner on the default ports would answer for a build that bound nothing, and the control that must score zero would score everything.
stories.requirements: Checked before the builder is called.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No attempt is ever scored against another attempt's app.
stories.qa_tests: A port probe reporting the seeded port taken makes the attempt raise, naming that port and that instance, with the builder never called.

stories.title: Send instance output to a file, never to an undrained pipe
stories.description: R25. A pipe holds 64 KiB; an app logging per request fills it partway through the walkthrough and stops answering, producing the zero control's ledger line from an app that works. And nothing is read to end-of-file, because a start script that backgrounds its server leaves the write end held by a grandchild and the read would hang past the budget with no verdict written.
stories.requirements: A file, and never a read to EOF.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A chatty app still serves, and a backgrounding script does not hang the runner.
stories.qa_tests: A build writing twenty thousand bytes per request, driven twenty times by the oracle, still scores — so a runner that goes back to an undrained pipe stalls and fails.

stories.title: Stop every instance by its process group
stories.description: R26. Even when the start script has already exited, because that is exactly the case where a server is left alive holding the port — and a leaked app is what makes the next attempt's score false.
stories.requirements: The group, not the script's pid.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nothing survives an attempt.
stories.qa_tests: A start script that backgrounds a long sleeper, records its pid and exits zero: the attempt is reported inside its budget and the sleeper is gone afterwards.

stories.title: Treat an instance that answers and then dies as a did-not-start
stories.description: R27. Between the two starts or during the walkthrough. Each instance is waited for in turn, so the first is up and unwatched for as long as the second takes to answer.
stories.requirements: Not scored.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A dying app does not produce a partial score.
stories.qa_tests: A build that serves briefly and exits three, with an oracle slow enough that it dies during the walkthrough, yields a did-not-start carrying the exit code and the instance's own last words.

stories.title: Distinguish a closed budget from a failed start
stories.description: R28. An app given two seconds of a four-hour window did not fail to start; it was never asked.
stories.requirements: Abandonment, not blame.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The runner never records a model failure that was its own scheduling.
stories.qa_tests: Inject a clock sitting a second short of the budget once the builder returns: the outcome is abandoned and the ledger says so.

stories.title: Guard both databases and both ports
stories.description: R29. A seeded database inside the reference app is refused; one that does not exist is refused rather than handed over as a silent four-mark tax; one that is the same file as the ordinary database is refused, because both instances would read undegraded data and the seeded behaviours would fail with nothing saying why. Two instances on one port are refused too, since the walkthrough would read the first one twice.
stories.requirements: The second database guarded like the first.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No configuration produces a silently wrong score.
stories.qa_tests: The entry point with a seeded database inside the reference app, with one that does not exist, and with one that is the ordinary database, each refuses. An attempt with both instances on one port raises.

stories.title: Stage the seeded copy and refuse a missing source
stories.description: R30. sqlite's connect creates a missing file, so a mistyped source leaves a real empty database at the typo forever and every run after the first is scored against empty data under a status that says it was measured. And a seeder that raises halfway must leave nothing at the final path, because a half-degraded database there is one a later run reuses.
stories.requirements: Refuse a missing source; stage and rename.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No typo becomes a permanent empty database, and no half-degraded copy survives.
stories.qa_tests: A copy from a path that does not exist raises without creating the file. A copy with a seeder that deletes a row and then raises leaves nothing at all at the final path.

features.title: Human feedback as signal
features.description: Daniel's reading of a rebuild is the only judgement in the loop that knows whether an app is any good as against merely conformant. It enters in three places, deliberately kept apart, because they have different costs and different half-lives.
features.requirements: R14: a comment that names a behaviour the app should have is turned into a new numbered behaviour in the manifest with a step to match, and then scores mechanically every night forever with no model involved — the cheapest and strongest form, and the default destination for feedback. R15: a comment about how something should have been built rather than what it should do becomes a line in the rubric the brief carries, so the next attempt reads it before it starts — cheap, immediate, and bounded by how much of the brief a small model actually attends to. R16: a comment that prefers one attempt over another becomes a preference pair — one brief, two attempts, Daniel's verdict and his reason — and the runner already keeps two attempts of one brief apart precisely so this is possible; these accumulate towards training and are useless in ones and twos, with the honest threshold being hundreds, so until then they are a dataset being built rather than a loop being closed. R17: every verdict is recorded against the attempt identifier it judged, with which of the three destinations it went to, so a rubric line can be traced back to the attempt that provoked it.
features.acceptance_criteria: Feedback defaults to the manifest, because that is the form that scores forever with no model involved.
features.qa_tests: Traceability is the testable part: a rubric line can be traced back to the attempt that provoked it, and a verdict is recorded against the attempt identifier it judged with its destination named.

stories.title: Turn a missing-behaviour comment into a numbered manifest behaviour
stories.description: R14. With a step to match, so it scores mechanically every night forever with no model involved. The default destination for feedback.
stories.requirements: A number and a step.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The behaviour is gradeable from the next run.
stories.qa_tests: A behaviour added this way appears in the next brief's gradeable set and in the next report. The parser refuses a duplicate number, so the addition has to be unique.

stories.title: Turn a how-it-should-be-built comment into a rubric line
stories.description: R15. Carried in the brief so the next attempt reads it before it starts. Bounded by how much of the brief a small model actually attends to.
stories.requirements: A line in the brief's rubric.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The next attempt reads it.
stories.qa_tests: The composed brief carries the line. Whether the model attends to it is read from the attempt rather than asserted.

stories.title: Record a preference between two attempts as a pair
stories.description: R16. One brief, two attempts, Daniel's verdict and his reason. The runner already keeps two attempts of one brief apart precisely so this is possible. Useless in ones and twos — the honest threshold is hundreds, so until then this is a dataset being built rather than a loop being closed.
stories.requirements: The verdict and the reason, against both attempt identifiers.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Pairs accumulate towards training.
stories.qa_tests: A pair references two distinct attempt identifiers from one brief and carries a reason. The dataset's usefulness is a question of volume rather than of a passing test.

stories.title: Record every verdict against its attempt and destination
stories.description: R17. So a rubric line can be traced back to the attempt that provoked it.
stories.requirements: The attempt identifier and which of the three destinations.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Any rubric line's origin is recoverable.
stories.qa_tests: A recorded verdict names the attempt it judged and its destination. A rubric line can be traced back to its provoking attempt.
